2.text: poor families usually combine for the summer and form a large herd with plenty

3.text: of herdsmen. Early in the fall the herds are separated; and in winter some

4.text: of the poor men will join their wealthy neighbors and help them watch the

5.text: herd, receiving for their pay some skins, and some animals for slaughter.

6.text: Such temporary helpers generally leave in spring, before the calving-season,

7.text: since at that time a large herd gives much trouble. It must be kept moving

8.text: in search of new pastures. Does with young ones are very slow. In a herd

9.text: of a thousand does there are some thirty calvings daily. The herdsman has

10.text: to keep his eye on every one of these. He leaves them behind, then comes

11.text: back for them, and even assists the inexperienced dam.

12.text: Many poor families, especially those who want to raise a herd of their

13.text: own, enter the service of one of their wealthy neighbors for several years.

14.text: They are very hard-worked, and receive as pay their meat-supply and skins

15.text: from the herd of their master; but in moving from camp to camp they must

16.text: use their own pack and driving animals. Meanwhile their own little stock is

17.text: left undisturbed to multiply. In return for good services, they may expect to

18.text: receive from their master every year about ten fawns; and with the natural

19.text: increase of their own animals they may secure one hundred reindeer in the

20.text: course of five fairly favorable years. Such helpers are called “dwelling-mates”

22.text: strive in every way to attract at least one poor family. Often these are poor

23.text: relatives of the owner of the herd. If there are any young unmarried men

24.text: in these families, they will be offered a girl of the master’s family in marriage,

25.text: and thus become relatives of his.

26.text: With the beginning of summer, when sledges become useless and tents

27.text: cannot be moved around the country, the Chukchee herdsmen usually leave

28.text: their families in camp, and move with the herd about twenty miles away, to

29.text: the summer pastures. Boys and girls of more than ten years, and young

30.text: women having no small children, usually go along for a time. While moving

31.text: about with the herd, the herdsmen have to carry on their backs all necessaries,

32.text: such as extra clothing, rifle and ammunition, kettles, and provisions. After

33.text: they have killed a reindeer, they must carry its skin and meat until it is

34.text: consumed. For this reason the herdsmen are so averse to slaughtering an

35.text: animal at that season, that they sometimes go for several days on starvation

36.text: rations. If the hoof-disease breaks out, they have plenty of meat, but they

37.text: have to carry along additional loads of skins. Sometimes they are so heavily

38.text: laden as to be hardly able to move. The burdens are carried by girls and

39.text: by men who are not very agile; while the best herdsmen must remain unen-

40.text: cumbered for moving swiftly around the herd.

42.text: the fall, are also hard on the herdsman; but the winter is easier, especially
